think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: An 11-year-old girl endured 13 months of recurrent fever, cough, chest pain, pulmonary abscess, pleural effusions, and massive exudative pericardial effusion requiring thoracotomy and partial pericardiectomy. She underwent prolonged empiric antibiotic and anti-tuberculosis regimens without improvement. The key diagnostic dilemma was distinguishing between atypical chronic bacterial empyema, disseminated tuberculosis with polyserositis, and a foodborne trematode infestation (paragonimiasis) masked by the absence of a recalled history of raw freshwater crustacean ingestion, but betrayed by persistent marked peripheral eosinophilia (up to 17%) in an individual native to Yunnan province.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint is established upon admission to the tertiary hospital, following physical examination, baseline CBC (showing marked eosinophilia), liver and kidney function tests, and repeat chest ultrasound and CT, but strictly prior to parasite-specific serology (ELISA) and anti-helminthic therapy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Bacterial lung abscess and purulent pericarditis were suspected based on suppurative thoracic disease and elevated CRP, but failed prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. Tuberculosis was considered given endemicity, lymphadenopathy, and serositis, but failed months of anti-tuberculosis therapy and multiple tuberculin/molecular tests (PPD, T-SPOT, smear, MTB PCR) were negative. Persistent marked eosinophilia in a patient from Yunnan province strongly pointed toward paragonimiasis.
case_prompt:
An 11-year-old girl is admitted with a 13-month history of worsening intermittent chest pain, cough, and fever. Her illness began 13 months prior with acute chest pain, fever, and cough. At initial evaluation elsewhere, she had leukocytosis (15.69 x 10^9/L), eosinophilia of 14.3%, thrombocytosis (456 x 10^9/L), and elevated C-reactive protein (150.6 mg/L). Initial chest imaging revealed a right middle and lower lobe pulmonary abscess, pleural thickening, small pleural effusion, and mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy. She underwent right exploratory thoracotomy for abscess clearance and received empiric antibiotics as well as four months of antimycobacterial medications (isoniazid and rifampicin) without clinical cure. Two months post-discharge, she developed severe chest pain and fever; echocardiography revealed a large exudative pericardial effusion (2.4 cm maximal diastolic separation), prompting video-assisted thoracoscopy and partial pericardiectomy, which demonstrated chronic suppurative inflammation and granulation tissue hyperplasia. Despite continued antimicrobial therapy, she suffered recurrent bouts of chest pain, fever, and cough over the subsequent five months. She denies a history of eating raw freshwater crabs or crayfish, but was born and raised in Yunnan province.

On physical examination, cardiac and pulmonary auscultation are normal. The abdomen is soft, and the liver and spleen are not palpable. There is no peripheral lymphadenopathy, and no subcutaneous nodules are identified.

Admission laboratory testing reveals a white blood cell count of 11.56 x 10^9/L with prominent eosinophilia of 17%. Renal and liver function tests are normal. Bedside chest ultrasonography demonstrates a shallow 0.5-mm left pleural effusion, while repeat chest CT shows no residual pericardial effusion following the prior pericardiectomy.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Bacterial lung abscess and purulent pericarditis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Initially suspected given suppurative lung cavitation, high CRP, and pericarditis; however, the patient failed multiple prolonged courses of broad-spectrum antibacterial therapy, and marked peripheral eosinophilia persisted.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A chest CT showed an abscess in the middle and lower lobes of the right lung, thickening of adjacent pleura, a small amount of pleural effusion... Antibiotics ceased to be effective after 4 months of treatment.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Empirically treated with dual-agent anti-tuberculosis drugs for several months without symptomatic remission, and extensive mycobacterial workups across hospitalizations remained consistently negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Pulmonary tuberculosis was considered, and anti-tuberculosis treatment (isoniazid and rifampicin) was administered for 4 months after admission... All tuberculosis-related tests (PPD test, T-spot, sputum smear for acidophilus and DNA of Mycobacterium tuberculosis) were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The combination of persistent high-grade peripheral eosinophilia (17%) and geographic exposure in Yunnan province established suspicion for a foodborne trematode; serum ELISA for Paragonimus was positive, and oral praziquantel resulted in rapid resolution of pleural effusion and complete cessation of chest pain and fevers.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: She had no history of ingesting freshwater crabs or crayfish, but was born in Yunnan province where paragonimiasis is a severe public health issue... white blood cell count of 11.56 x 109/L and eosinophils of up to 17% were noted... ELISA for Paragonimus was positive, which confirmed the diagnosis of paragonimiasis. She was given 600 mg of praziquantel 3 times a day.

editor_comments: Distilled strictly per Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Zero mention of Paragonimus or anti-helminthic therapy in the case prompt, preserving eosinophilia and geographic exposure as key diagnostic cues.
